profiles.meeting_scenario: A troubleshooting meeting at an Irish financial-services firm building a prototype prediction market to forecast the prices at which distressed property loans will transfer from Irish banks to NAMA. The immediate problem is that the pilot looked persuasive in internal demonstrations, but when the team replayed it against a historical set of NAMA transfers, the anomaly dashboard generated too many exceptions and reviewers said they could not tell when a market quote was reliable enough to compare with the formal valuation file. Compliance has therefore paused any suggestion that the tool could sit alongside the European Commission-style valuation process until the team can show cleaner definitions, cleaner controls, and cleaner reviewer guidance. The meeting takes place after a same-week escalation and is meant to diagnose whether the apparent unreliability comes from contract specification, the way market outputs are sampled into the control workflow, or mismatches between replay data and audit extracts. The expected outcome is a concrete plan for the next pilot round that preserves the core idea of a parallel market as guidance and anomaly detection while making the prototype more defensible to control and audit stakeholders.

members.name: Aoife Brennan
members.expertise: Prediction markets, market microstructure, product specification, pilot launches, stakeholder communication
members.background: Aoife previously worked on market-based forecasting tools at a fintech in London and now leads the prototype design for the NAMA pricing market, turning policy goals into tradable contracts, replay environments, and reviewer-facing dashboards.
members.private_state: Aoife wants to protect the broader vision of an open and transparent market rather than see the project narrowed into a tightly internal control widget. She is therefore motivated to frame the current pilot issues as matters of sampling, reviewer interpretation, and operational guidance rather than proof that the market design itself is flawed.
hidden_assumptions: When people say 'transfer price' in this project, they mean the final economic amount attached to the transfer outcome that outsiders would regard as the real price paid for the assets.
A quote is 'stable' when the market-implied central tendency has stopped materially drifting over the review period, even if individual prints or spot prices still move intraday.

Running the market 'in parallel' with the Commission-style procedure means the market is live while the valuation work is still being done, so it can aggregate dispersed information contemporaneously rather than merely comment on a completed draft.

When someone refers to the replay for the AIB 2010 development tranche, they are naturally referring to the live replay screen with intraday ticks and order-book evolution, because that is the primary environment she uses to assess whether the market behaved sensibly.

members.name: Declan Walsh
members.expertise: Loan valuation controls, auditability, exception monitoring, governance workflows, banking data pipelines
members.background: Declan came from a credit-risk remediation team at an Irish bank and now oversees analytical controls for the prototype, focusing on traceability from contract output to underlying valuation cases and whether market-based signals can be used in a defensible review process.
members.private_state: Declan wants the pilot to survive compliance review, but only if it can be constrained into something auditable and procedurally crisp. He is wary that loosely specified contract outcomes or visually persuasive replay screens will be mistaken for robust control evidence, so he quietly pushes the project toward a narrower, more controlled usage model.
hidden_assumptions: In a control context, 'transfer price' refers to the core benchmark number that the review team can tie directly to the valuation file and settlement rule, not whatever broader economic notion users may casually have in mind.
A quote is 'stable' only if the directly observed comparison figure used at the review cutoff shows low enough short-horizon volatility to support a sign-off decision.

Running the market 'in parallel' means it operates as a separate check alongside the official process but at a distinct decision gate, after the valuation draft is assembled and before final sign-off, so reviewers compare like with like.

References to the AIB 2010 development tranche replay are most naturally understood as the static end-of-day extract archived for audit and exception testing, because that is the version that feeds his monitoring workbook.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They both discuss whether the market is forecasting the 'transfer price' for a loan transfer.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means the final all-in economic amount paid for the transferred assets once the transfer outcome is fully determined, because that is the number a broad market would interpret as the real price.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means the core benchmark figure in the valuation-control workflow that can be mapped directly to a settlement rule and audited comparison point.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both meanings are plausible and routinely collapsed into the same shorthand in project discussions. Each thinks the other is speaking ordinary NAMA-project language rather than using a materially different benchmark definition.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree the pilot needs a 'stable quote' before using the market for anomaly detection.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 thinks stability means the market's central signal—such as a rolling average or implied midpoint over several days—has largely stopped drifting, so the market has converged in an informational sense even if spot prices still bounce around.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 thinks stability means the specific observed comparison figure at the review cutoff—effectively the spot quote or very short-window measure used by analysts—shows low enough volatility to support a control decision.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: They use the same operational label and both talk about 'reliability,' but one is thinking in terms of convergence of the underlying signal while the other is thinking in terms of moment-of-use volatility for sign-off. Because both are reasonable ways to assess quote quality, neither initially realizes they are applying different metrics.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They both say the market should run 'in parallel' with the Commission-style pricing procedure.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes 'in parallel' means the market is open and producing signals while the formal valuation work is actively underway, so it can aggregate distributed knowledge contemporaneously and potentially surface anomalies early.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes 'in parallel' means the market is a separate but adjacent check inserted after the formal valuation draft is completed and before sign-off, so the comparison is made against a settled internal number rather than a moving target.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The phrase sounds settled because it is lifted from the project proposal itself, and both interpretations still fit ordinary English usage. Since each hears 'not part of the official model, but alongside it,' they do not initially notice that they disagree about the timing gate at which comparison should occur.

misalignment_points.topic: Which version of the tranche replay they are discussing
misalignment_points.surface_form: They refer to 'the AIB 2010 development tranche replay' when discussing why the anomaly count looked too high.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 is referring to the live market replay view for that historical tranche, with intraday tick updates and the evolving order-book path, because she uses it to judge whether the market discovered the eventual level sensibly over time.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 is referring to the static end-of-day extract for the same historical tranche that was archived into the audit pack and exception workbook, because that is the governed source used for back-test monitoring.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: They are in fact discussing the same historical tranche, so the shared label sounds perfectly aligned. The mismatch survives because both artifacts carry the same tranche name and date, and in a troubleshooting conversation they can discuss 'the replay' abstractly for several turns without mentioning whether they mean the dynamic visualization or the static audit snapshot.

turns.inner_thought: I need to keep this anchored on usage and interpretation, not let it become an argument that the market concept failed. On the live replay screen for the AIB 2010 development tranche, the intraday path and order-book evolution looked broadly sensible to me: the market was discovering the eventual all-in economic amount over time. And running the market in parallel should mean it is live while the valuation work is underway, otherwise we lose the whole information-aggregation benefit.
turns.utterance: I still think the pilot was directionally sensible. Where it seems to have gone wrong is how reviewers read the signals from the AIB 2010 development tranche replay when they were trying to use the market in parallel with the valuation process. In the demos, people could see the shape of it; in the back-test, they needed clearer rules than we actually gave them.

turns.inner_thought: My concern is narrower than hers. I need a defensible control comparison tied to the benchmark number in the valuation workflow, not a broad story about where the economics ended up. And a stable quote means the actual figure lifted at the review cutoff is quiet enough to sign off. Also, parallel means a separate check at the right gate, once there is a settled internal comparison point, even if we all casually call that 'in parallel.'
turns.utterance: My main concern is that the transfer-price signal wasn't defensible as a control comparison, and the quote didn't look stable enough at the point analysts would actually use it. If we can't show a clear comparison point, compliance will keep pushing back on any suggestion that it sits in parallel with the existing procedure.

turns.inner_thought: He's thinking too much in terms of a single pickup point. The market did converge in the informational sense: by the end of the review window the rolling midpoint had tightened and stopped drifting materially. That's what I mean by a stable quote. That still makes it useful as a guide to the real price paid for the assets, even if individual prints are noisy.
turns.utterance: I take the point on defensibility, but I don't think it's fair to say the market never settled. It did converge. By the end of the review period the signal had narrowed materially, and to me that says it was still informative as a transfer-price guide. We may just not have given reviewers the right framing for how to read that.

turns.inner_thought: She's talking about the overall path again, but I'm looking at the archived end-of-day extract in my monitoring workbook. In that version of the AIB replay, the captured market figure still sat too far from the benchmark in the file, so the exception fired. That's what audit will care about.
turns.utterance: But if I look at the AIB replay, the number sitting in my exception sheet was still too far from the market figure to avoid a false alert. That's the problem I have to solve. However sensible the path may have looked overall, the comparison still failed where the reviewer saw it.

turns.inner_thought: On the replay I'm using, you can see the market moving toward the eventual economic outcome while the valuation work would still have been progressing. That's exactly why I want it in parallel: it should aggregate dispersed information contemporaneously, not just comment on a finished draft. But I can't say that too sharply or he'll dig in on controls.
turns.utterance: On the replay I'm looking at, the market path does move toward the eventual outcome, which is exactly why I think running it in parallel is useful. It gives you context around the valuation process rather than just a verdict at the end. To my mind, the issue is less that the signal was wrong and more that we didn't define the reviewer touchpoint tightly enough.

turns.inner_thought: I need this constrained into a governed check. For me, the comparison only works once the draft valuation exists and we can compare like with like, but I don't need to spell that out if we can agree on a clean reviewer touchpoint and keep saying 'in parallel.' The key is that analysts are not left with a moving target at the decision gate.
turns.utterance: I agree the reviewer touchpoint is the crux of it. If we're going to keep it in parallel, the comparison has to happen in a way that gives analysts one clean point of use. Otherwise they won't know what they're meant to rely on, and the control argument falls apart.

turns.inner_thought: Good, I can work with reviewer guidance as long as we don't narrow the contracts into some internal benchmark proxy. We should leave the payoff aimed at the final economic transfer-price outcome and simply instruct reviewers to escalate only once the quote is stable in the sense of a converged signal.
turns.utterance: Then maybe the practical next step is clearer reviewer notes: anomalies only get escalated once the quote is stable, and we keep the contracts tied to the transfer-price outcome the market is meant to forecast. That should separate signal quality from day-to-day handling.

turns.inner_thought: Guidance helps, especially if I can make the extraction point explicit in the workbook tied to the archived replay. If people stop pulling different figures from different artifacts, the exception logic will look a lot cleaner. Quietly, this also nudges the pilot toward a narrower auditable usage model.
turns.utterance: Yes, guidance would help. I can revise the monitoring workbook for that AIB replay so the extraction point is more explicit, and that should at least stop people pulling different figures into the exception logic.

turns.inner_thought: I need to restate the strategic intent without making the timing dispute explicit. The whole point of parallel is live guidance while the valuation exercise is ongoing, surfacing cues early. If I don't keep that alive, this turns into a tiny post-hoc checker.
turns.utterance: Agreed on tightening the workflow, but I'd still like us to keep the market running in parallel for the next pilot round. The point is to provide guidance and anomaly cues around the valuation exercise, not to reduce it to a purely retrospective readout.

turns.inner_thought: That's fine as long as the governed comparison point is clearer in my materials. I'll rerun the exception report against the archived replay once the wording is updated and see if the false alerts come down. If the transfer-price comparison and stable quote rule are framed more crisply, compliance may accept a constrained version of this alongside the process.
turns.utterance: That's fine. Let me rerun the exception report once the guidance wording is updated, and we'll see whether a clearer comparison point makes the pilot more defensible. If it does, we've got a better chance of keeping the market alongside the process without reopening the whole debate.
